38239:
Who were 'the Galatians'? The name originally meant the Celtic tribes who settled in north-central Asia Minor around 278 BC. But from 25 BC 'Galatia' was also the name of a large Roman province that included cities further south, such as Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, which Paul and Barnabas evangelised on the first journey (Acts 13-14). The North Galatian theory, the older majority view and still favoured by many German and some English scholars (J. B. Lightfoot, J. Louis Martyn), holds that Paul wrote to ethnic Galatians in the north, perhaps visited on the journeys of Acts 16:6 and Acts 18:23, and that the letter dates from the mid-50s. The South Galatian theory, argued powerfully by William Ramsay and held by many English-speaking evangelical scholars (F. F. Bruce, Richard Longenecker, Craig Keener), holds that Paul wrote to the southern churches, perhaps as early as 48-49. The question is genuinely open.

The date matters because of how Galatians relates to Acts 15. If Galatians was written before the Jerusalem council, it would be Paul's earliest letter, and his silence about the council's ruling would be natural; the Jerusalem visit of Galatians 2:1-10 would then be the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30. If it was written after, Galatians 2 probably describes the council itself from Paul's angle.

Either way, the issue is clear. Gentiles who turned from idols to Israel's God through Jesus were in an odd position: they were neither pagans nor Jews. Pagan neighbours saw them abandon the city's gods, which was dangerous; Jewish neighbours saw uncircumcised men claiming to belong to Abraham's God. Circumcision would regularise their position, making them proselytes, legally recognisable members of a Jewish community and safer from persecution (Gal 6:12). The teachers probably argued from Genesis 17, where God commands circumcision for Abraham's household as an everlasting covenant. Paul replies from Genesis 15, where Abraham trusted God and was counted righteous before he was circumcised, and from the Galatians' own experience of receiving the Spirit without the Law (Gal 3:2-5).
38240: Circumcision as covenant sign and social identity
38241: For Jews circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, commanded in Genesis 17. For Gentile men it was a painful adult operation that publicly made them Jews. It was the decisive boundary marker between Israel and the nations.
38243: Many Jews avoided eating with Gentiles because of food laws and fear of idolatry. In Antioch Peter ate with Gentile believers until people from James arrived, then withdrew. Paul saw this as splitting the one family of God at the meal table, the most visible sign of belonging.
38245: A household slave who escorted a boy to school and supervised his behaviour until he came of age. Paul says the Law was Israel's paidagōgos until Christ came: a protective, temporary guardian, not an enemy.
38247: Under Roman and Greek law an heir who was still a minor had no more freedom than a slave until the date set by his father. Paul uses this to say that both Jews and Gentiles have now come of age as God's sons, with the Spirit crying 'Abba'.
38248: Honour, curse and the evil eye
38249: 'Who has bewitched you?' (Gal 3:1) uses the language of the evil eye, a widely feared form of envious magic. Paul's curse formula (Gal 1:8-9) and his line about the Galatians once willing to tear out their eyes for him (Gal 4:15) work within this honour-and-curse world.
38251: Letters were usually dictated to a scribe; the sender might add a closing in his own writing as a signature and guarantee. Paul's 'large letters' underline the seriousness of his final appeal.
38252:
Galatians is often read as Paul against Judaism. Read in its setting, it is an argument between Jewish believers in Jesus about how Gentiles share Israel's blessings. Paul does not say Jews must stop being Jews; he himself says 'we ourselves are Jews by birth' (Gal 2:15). He is arguing that Gentiles must not become Jews in order to be counted members of Abraham's family, because God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed in him (Gen 12:3, Gal 3:8). If Gentiles had to be circumcised, the promise would only ever produce one nation, not the blessing of many.

The New Perspective on Paul (James Dunn, N. T. Wright) reads 'works of the law' here as the practices that marked Jews out from Gentiles, especially circumcision, food laws and calendar. Paul's opposition is to making those badges the test of membership. The 'Paul within Judaism' scholars (Mark Nanos, Matthew Thiessen, Paula Fredriksen) argue that Paul assumed Jewish believers would keep Torah, and that his objection was specifically to Gentiles being circumcised, which Thiessen argues many Jews themselves thought could not make a Gentile a true descendant of Abraham. Traditional Reformed and Lutheran readers (Thomas Schreiner, Stephen Westerholm, Douglas Moo) accept that boundary markers are in view but argue that Paul's logic goes deeper: no human doing of the Law, of any kind, can make anyone right with God, since the Law pronounces a curse on all who fail to keep it (Gal 3:10).

Paul's key texts are all Jewish Scripture: Abraham's faith (Gen 15:6), the curse of Deuteronomy, Habakkuk's 'the righteous shall live by faith' (Hab 2:4), Isaiah's barren woman who rejoices (Isa 54:1). Even the most controversial passage, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah (Gal 4:21-31), is a Jewish-style midrash. It does not say Jews are Hagar's children; it contrasts two ways of belonging: through human effort to secure status (Hagar and Ishmael born 'by the flesh') or through God's promise and the Spirit. Reading it as Judaism versus Christianity misses that Paul addresses Gentiles being tempted to seek status by circumcision.
38253: Paul skips his usual thanksgiving and curses any message that adds conditions to the gospel of grace.
38255: His gospel came by revelation, not from Jerusalem, yet the pillars recognised it and shook hands.
38257: Peter's withdrawal from Gentile tables denies that both are justified by faith in Christ, and Paul opposes him to his face.
38259: The Spirit came by hearing with faith; Abraham was counted righteous by trust, and in Christ the blessing reaches the nations.
38261: The Law came 430 years after the promise and guarded Israel until Christ; now all are one in him, heirs by promise.
38263: A personal appeal, then Hagar and Sarah: children of the promise must not return to slavery.
38265: Stand firm in freedom, serve each other in love, walk by the Spirit and bear one another's burdens.
38266: New creation in his own hand
38267: Circumcision is not the issue; new creation is. Peace on the Israel of God.
38268: One family of Abraham by faith and Spirit
38289: Doing what the Torah requires. Traditional readers take it as obeying the Law to earn standing with God; New Perspective readers stress the identity markers of circumcision, food and Sabbath that separated Jews and Gentiles. Both readings see Paul denying that these justify.
38290: Trust and loyalty. The phrase pistis Christou (Gal 2:16, Gal 2:20) may mean 'faith in Christ' or 'the faithfulness of Christ', a long-running debate (Richard Hays for the latter, James Dunn and Moo for the former).
38292: To declare in the right. In Galatians the question is who counts as a member of God's righteous people and on what basis, which includes standing before God's judgement.
38294: God's commitment to Abraham, which Paul says the later Law cannot annul. The promised blessing is identified with the Spirit.
38296: Not simply the body but human life apart from God's Spirit, including religious self-reliance ('make a good showing in the flesh') and selfish desires.
38297: Paul's whole argument hangs on Abraham: the promise to bless the nations, faith counted as righteousness, and the stories of Hagar and Sarah.
38298: Acts 15 records the Jerusalem council on the same issue; how Galatians 2 fits Acts 11 and 15 is central to the dating debate.
38299: Romans develops the same themes with less heat and adds Israel's future (Rom 9-11).
38300: Paul cites Deuteronomy's curse on all who do not keep the whole Law, and the curse on one hanged on a tree, which Christ bore.
38301: 'The righteous will live by faith' is quoted against reliance on the Law.
38302: James insists faith without works is dead; many see him correcting a misuse of Paul, not Paul himself.
38303: Christ is the one who 'gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age' (Gal 1:4). He 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us' (Gal 3:13), the single 'seed' of Abraham in whom the promise is fulfilled (Gal 3:16), and the Son sent 'born of a woman, born under the law' (Gal 4:4). Paul's most personal confession is here: 'I have been crucified with Christ... the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me' (Gal 2:20). Christian tradition has used Galatians to defend salvation by grace through faith; Jewish readers note that Paul's claim is not that Israel's God has changed but that, in the Messiah, God has begun the promised blessing of the nations.
38304: 'Works of the law' as good deeds or moral effort in general
38305: When Paul says no one is justified by 'works of the law' (Gal 2:16), he means trying to earn salvation by being good: going to church, giving, doing good deeds. The Judaizers taught salvation by human effort, like any religion of works.
38306: James Dunn and N. T. Wright argue that the phrase refers first to the Torah's specific requirements, and in Galatians especially to those that separated Jews from Gentiles: circumcision, food laws and holy days, which are exactly what is at stake in Gal 2:3, Gal 2:12 and Gal 4:10. E. P. Sanders showed that Judaism did not generally teach that one earns entry into God's favour by merit; one was in the covenant by God's grace and kept the Law as a response. So the Galatian dispute was about who belongs to Abraham's family and on what terms, not about whether moral effort can buy heaven.
38307: Stephen Westerholm, Simon Gathercole, Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner reply that 'works of the law' does mean the whole Law, not only badges (Gal 3:10 speaks of 'all things written in the book of the law'), and that Paul's logic generalises: if the God-given Torah cannot justify, no human performance can. Gathercole shows that some Jewish texts did expect final vindication partly on the basis of obedience. Most scholars now agree that the popular picture of Jews as self-righteous merit-earners is a caricature, while disagreeing about how far Paul's principle extends to all human works. Ephesians 2:8-9 and Titus 3:5, which speak of 'works' generally, are often cited by the traditional side.
38308: The traditional reading guards grace against moralism. The New Perspective reading guards against turning religion into ethnic or cultural badges that exclude others, and corrects an unfair picture of Judaism. Both concerns are real.
38309: Galatians 3:28 as either only spiritual or as abolishing all differences
38310: Two popular readings collide. One says 'neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female' is only about equal access to salvation and has no social implications. The other says it abolishes all distinctions, so ethnicity and gender no longer matter at all.
38311: In context the verse is about the baptised being 'one' family and heirs of Abraham (Gal 3:26-29), and it immediately had social effects: Jews and Gentiles eating together (Gal 2:11-14). Paul still speaks of Jews and Gentiles, men and women, so the distinctions remain but no longer rank people before God or divide the table. Scholars such as Richard Longenecker and Craig Keener see it as a programme that the church gradually worked out.
38312: Complementarian scholars agree the verse has social implications (it rules out ethnic or class favouritism) but argue that it addresses who inherits, not what roles men and women have in church leadership. Egalitarian scholars argue its logic does extend to roles. Both agree it is more than a private spiritual equality.
38313: The verse was central to debates over slavery, racial segregation in churches and women's ministry; reading it in context keeps it from being either emptied or stretched beyond Paul's point.
38314: Gentile converts in Galatia, under social pressure and confused by persuasive teachers, were told that they already fully belonged to God's family through Christ and the Spirit, and that the Spirit's fruit, not circumcision, marked them out.
38315: Galatians shaped Luther and the Reformation's 'by faith alone'. Today it also speaks to churches that make cultural customs, political loyalties or denominational markers into tests of who truly belongs, and to believers who feel they must earn God's acceptance.
38316: Ephesians celebrates God's plan to unite everything in Christ, starting with a new people in which Jews and Gentiles are reconciled, and calls that people to live it out in unity, holiness and households shaped by Christ.
38318: Presented as Paul writing as 'a prisoner for the Lord' (Eph 4:1), sending Tychicus with news (Eph 6:21-22). If not by Paul, it was written by a close disciple who knew Colossians well and wanted to sum up Paul's teaching for a new generation.
38319: The letter claims Paul (Eph 1:1, Eph 3:1) and was accepted as his from the second century. Doubts arise from its long liturgical sentences (Eph 1:3-14 is one sentence in Greek), vocabulary, the stress on the universal church and on salvation as already accomplished, and its heavy overlap with Colossians. Scholars such as Andrew Lincoln and Margaret MacDonald think it is post-Pauline; Harold Hoehner, Clinton Arnold and Peter O'Brien defend Paul. Opinion is divided, perhaps roughly evenly among all scholars.
38321: The writer is in chains (Eph 6:20). Tradition places this in Paul's Roman house arrest (Acts 28:30-31); some propose Caesarea or Ephesus. If the letter is post-Pauline, the prison setting is part of its presentation of Paul.
38322: Gentile believers in the province of Asia, probably several churches
38323: Ephesus and surrounding cities of Asia
38324: The words 'in Ephesus' (Eph 1:1) are missing from the earliest manuscripts (Papyrus 46, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus), and the letter contains no personal greetings, odd for a church where Paul spent nearly three years. Many think it was a circular letter for several churches. The readers are Gentiles ('you who were once far off', Eph 2:13) who needed to know their place in God's people and how to live in a city full of magic and powers.
38325: Approximate start of Paul's long ministry in Ephesus, teaching in the lecture hall of Tyrannus (Acts 19:9-10).
38326: Ephesian believers burn magic books worth 50,000 silver coins; the silversmiths riot in the theatre (Acts 19:19-41).
38327: Paul arrives in Rome under guard and lives two years under house arrest (Acts 28:16, Acts 28:30).
38328: James the brother of Jesus is executed in Jerusalem (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1).
38329: The Jerusalem temple is destroyed; if Ephesians is post-Pauline, its image of the church as a holy temple (Eph 2:21) would read differently after this.
38330:
Ephesus was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, a port of perhaps 200,000 people, with a theatre seating about 25,000 and the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. The city was famous for magic; 'Ephesian letters' were written charms, and Acts describes converts burning their magic scrolls (Acts 19:19). Its large Jewish community had protected rights. Paul spent between two and three years here (Acts 19:8-10, Acts 20:31), and the gospel spread through the region, to Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis.

If the letter was circular, it was written for Gentile believers across this region, people who had been 'without God in the world' (Eph 2:12) and had lived in fear of spiritual 'principalities and powers'. Ephesians answers that fear by showing Christ seated far above every power (Eph 1:20-22) and the church seated with him (Eph 2:6). Clinton Arnold's research on magic and power in Asia Minor shows how strongly this would have spoken to former users of charms and astrology.

Ephesians also addresses a social problem: how could Jews and Gentiles form one community when the temple in Jerusalem had a stone barrier forbidding Gentiles to go further on pain of death? Two inscriptions from that barrier have been found. Ephesians says that Christ 'has broken down the dividing wall of hostility' (Eph 2:14). Acts tells that Paul was arrested in Jerusalem after being accused of bringing Trophimus the Ephesian past that barrier (Acts 21:28-29), which gives the image a personal edge if Paul wrote it.
38332: A low stone balustrade in the Jerusalem temple courts carried warnings in Greek and Latin that any foreigner going beyond it would be responsible for his own death. Ephesians uses this as a picture of the hostility between Jew and Gentile that Christ abolished.
38334: People in Asia believed in many spiritual powers (rulers, authorities, cosmic forces) that could be manipulated by magic or astrology. Ephesians names these powers repeatedly and places them under Christ.
38335: Greek moral writers from Aristotle onwards taught 'household management' in three pairs: husbands and wives, fathers and children, masters and slaves, always addressing the male head. Ephesians follows this form but speaks directly to wives, children and slaves as moral agents, and frames everything with mutual submission and Christ's self-giving love.
38337: Cities granted citizenship as a high honour; resident foreigners lived without full rights. Gentiles in Christ are no longer 'strangers and aliens' but fellow citizens with God's holy people and members of his household.
38339: Readers saw Roman soldiers every day. But the armour of God draws mostly on Isaiah, where God himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet, so believers wear God's own armour.
38340:
Ephesians is written to Gentiles, but its world is Jewish. It opens with a long berakah, a Jewish blessing formula ('Blessed be the God and Father...'), like synagogue prayers that bless God for his deeds (Eph 1:3-14). The themes are Israel's: election, redemption, inheritance, God's people as 'his possession', the sealing of the Spirit as the down payment of the promised inheritance.

The centre is Ephesians 2:11-22. Gentiles were once 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise' (Eph 2:12). In Christ they have been 'brought near', language Isaiah uses for peace to the far and the near (Isa 57:19). They are not added to a new, non-Jewish religion; they are made fellow citizens with the holy ones and built into a single temple with the apostles and prophets as its foundation. The phrase 'one new man' (Eph 2:15) has sometimes been read as replacing Israel with a Gentile church. Scholars sensitive to Jewish identity (Markus Barth, Lynn Cohick) argue instead that Jews remain Jews and Gentiles remain Gentiles, reconciled in one body without either being erased.

The statement that Christ 'abolished the law of commandments in ordinances' (Eph 2:15) is also debated. Traditional readers see the ceremonial Law as fulfilled and set aside. New Perspective readers stress that what is abolished is the Law's function of dividing people, and 'Paul within Judaism' readers note that the letter is addressed to Gentiles and says nothing about Jews giving up Torah. The 'mystery' revealed to Paul (Eph 3:6) is not that God loves Gentiles, which the prophets already said, but that Gentiles share fully and equally in Israel's inheritance through the Messiah.
38341: A great Jewish-style blessing for election, redemption and the Spirit's seal, aiming to unite all things in Christ.
38343: Paul prays they will grasp the power that raised Christ and seated him over every authority, as head of the church.
38345: Dead in sins and under the powers, believers have been made alive and seated with Christ, by grace through faith, for good works.
38347: Gentiles once far off are now fellow citizens with Israel's holy ones, built into one temple.
38349: Paul's mission reveals the mystery of the Gentiles as co-heirs; he prays they know Christ's love beyond knowledge.
38351: One body, one Spirit; Christ's gifts equip the church to grow up together into maturity.
38353: Put off the old self, walk in love and light, and let mutual submission shape marriage, parenting and work.
38355: The struggle is against spiritual powers; stand firm in God's own armour and pray.
38382: In Ephesians the word usually means the whole worldwide church, Christ's body and bride, rather than one local gathering.
38384: God's unearned gift that raises the dead; it also gives each believer a share in ministry.
38386: Not a puzzle but a hidden purpose of God now revealed, especially that Gentiles share Israel's inheritance in Christ.
38387: The church as the body of which Christ is head, growing together as each part works.
38389: To gather everything under one head, as in summing up an argument. God's plan is to unite all things in heaven and earth in Christ.
38390: About a third of Ephesians' content has close parallels in Colossians, including the household code and the sending of Tychicus.
38391: Peace to the far and near, and the armour God himself wears, both come from Isaiah.
38392: Christ's ascent and giving of gifts is read through Psalm 68, and his rule through Psalm 110.
38393: Acts tells of Paul's long ministry in Ephesus and his farewell to the Ephesian elders.
38394: The 'one flesh' of marriage is applied to Christ and the church.
38395: The risen Christ's later letter to Ephesus praises the church's doctrinal vigilance but says it has lost its first love.
38396: Ephesians presents Christ as the one in whom God's whole plan for the universe comes together (Eph 1:10). He is the risen Lord seated at God's right hand above every power (Eph 1:20-21), the cornerstone of a new temple (Eph 2:20), 'our peace' who made Jew and Gentile one (Eph 2:14), the giver of gifts after his ascension (Eph 4:8-11) and the bridegroom who gave himself for his bride (Eph 5:25). Christian tradition draws on Ephesians for its doctrines of grace (Eph 2:8-9) and of the church. Jewish readers notice that Gentiles are said to be joined to the 'commonwealth of Israel', which suggests that, for this writer, the Messiah gathers the nations into Israel's hope rather than leaving Israel behind.
38398: Ephesians 2 is about how an individual is saved: by grace through faith, not by works. Verses 8-9 are the key; what follows about Jews and Gentiles is a secondary application.
